data.title: How Quantinuum's CEO Rajeeb Hazra Plans to Win Quantum Computing's Long Game — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Mackenzie Tatananni

Wall Street may be skeptical of an industry whose biggest payoffs could still be a decade away. But beneath the volatility, Quantinuum is positioning itself for quantum computing's long game.

Shares of the quantum developer have tumbled 51% since its public listing in June. Quantinuum debuted to heavy fanfare as the first traditional initial public offering in the quantum-computing industry and a long-awaited spinout from Honeywell International, which maintains a major equity stake.

Even as Quantinuum makes steady progress on the technical and commercial fronts, it hasn't been enough to stop the bruising slide. Still, CEO Rajeeb Hazra isn't sweating the share price.

"I think the stock price is not an indicator today of the value we create," Hazra said in an interview with Barron's. "The important thing is who is doing the three things right: building the right hardware, building the right software ecosystem, and engaging customers. That is where we are going to unlock hundreds of billions of value."

Reaching those figures will take time. Boston Consulting Group projects quantum computing will generate up to $850 billion in economic value by 2040. McKinsey's more bullish forecast places the potential value between $1.3 trillion and $2.7 trillion as early as 2035.

Against that distant horizon, Quantinuum's latest quarter marked another step forward. In its second report since going public, revenue more than tripled to $9.1 million, alongside a narrower per-share loss than analysts anticipated.

That momentum reflects a shift in how customers are buying into the technology. Two or three years ago, Hazra noted, commercial traction was largely limited to small, one-off partnerships. Today, deals are substantially larger and longer, spanning successive hardware generations. Chief among them in the latest quarter was a multi-year expansion with a client described only as a "global financial institution," marking the largest cloud contract in Quantinuum's history.

"We're seeing this model play out with other customers as well, which is, 'We've done our experimentation, now here's the business problem,'" Hazra said.

Interest is building ahead of next year's rollout of Quantinuum's fourth-generation system, Sol. That machine is scheduled to be followed in 2029 by Apollo, a fault-tolerant system that aligns with broader industry timelines targeting fault-tolerant computing by the end of the decade.

A fault-tolerant quantum computer, in simple terms, is one that catches and corrects physical errors in real time. A computer will never be entirely error-free — as is the case with today's classical machines — but quantum systems are particularly sensitive to noise from the environment, anything from temperature fluctuations to tiny vibrations, that threaten to bungle computations.

Quantinuum is taking steps to bring fault-tolerance to users with an overhaul of its Nexus platform, designed to simplify quantum application development, automate error correction, and carry these capabilities over across successive generations of hardware.

Usage of the platform accelerated in the third quarter, with adoption growing nearly 20% sequentially to 215 organizations. While "it's still a small number," it's a sign users want an effective way to program quantum machines, Hazra said. "It gives the industry a sort of predictability, and that's important because nobody in the software industry wants to write throwaway code."

Ultimately, Quantinuum sees its role as helping build the ecosystem and preparing for an industry that continues to mature. Yet even as timelines for fault-tolerant systems converge around the end of the decade, the industry still lacks consensus on proper standards to gauge technical progress.

There have been efforts on the federal front. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, an arm of the Defense Department, has been running an aptly named benchmarking initiative to gauge its participants' progress toward building a useful, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2033. Quantinuum expects to advance to the final stage, joining industry peers IBM, IonQ, Diraq, and Atom Computing.

Concurrently, Quantinuum and its partners have been working to advance a benchmarking framework dubbed Quantum Universal Operations Performance System, or QUOPS.

Historically, companies touted the raw physical qubit counts of their quantum computers, regardless of whether operations frequently failed due to the fragile nature of the underlying hardware. However, attention has shifted toward error correction, now recognized as an essential hurdle to bringing useful systems to market.

"I've always said the quantum industry is rife with claims. Now the doers versus the sayers will separate," Hazra said. "And it will really separate on the basis of customer choices, and things like the QuOps benchmark actually help crystallize it."

In an industry often mistakenly characterized as a winner-take-all race, Hazra acknowledges that no single company can shape the future of quantum in isolation. "We have no pride of ownership, but we have pride that we are moving the industry to where it needs to be in terms of having a benchmark," Hazra said. "Just like the classical industry, there will have to be competition and cooperation."

In time, Quantinuum's progress could be enough to convince Wall Street, rendering today's skepticism as nothing more than temporary noise.

Write to Mackenzie Tatananni at mackenzie.tatananni@barrons.com

data.title: Calley Means accuses Wiles of putting fundraising over MAHA agenda
data.description:
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, whose last day in that position is today, may have angered more than President Trump. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was likely not a fan either.

In an interview Friday with podcaster Joe Rogan, Calley Means, a senior advisor to RFK Jr. who quit last month, accused Wiles of putting fundraising from special interests opposed to health food policies ahead of the Make America Healthy Again agenda.

"Susie said to me many times: 'We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms,'" Means told Rogan.

In the two-hour interview, Means said Wiles declined to support plans to make children’s diets healthier due to money required from the sugar lobby, The New York Times reported.

He also said Wiles wanted more approvals of flavored e-cigarettes, a nod to the tobacco industry.

Wiles also criticized a Trump executive order encouraging production of glyphosate, the key ingredient in Bayer's herbicide Roundup, that is linked to cancer.

After a Wiles aide called Means to say that the EO was not up for debate with RFK Jr., Means said, "Susie then called Bobby’s office and said, 'We're not discussing this.'"

data.title: CBOT soybeans rebound from 12-week low
data.description:
Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures edged higher on Friday in a rebound from a 12-week low, though expectations for a record-large US harvest hung over the market, analysts said.

  • The US Department of Agriculture is expected to raise its estimate of US soybean production to 4.597 billion bushels in a monthly report due on Tuesday, up from 4.562 billion in October, according to a Reuters poll.

  • On Monday, the USDA is slated to issue a weekly update on harvesting progress, which was 88% complete as of November 1.

  • The USDA said on Friday that exporters sold 136,000 metric tons of US soybeans to top importer China for 2026/27 delivery.

  • "There is little that this market is grabbing onto from the bullish side as Chinese interest continues, but volumes appear light and South America weather forecasts are decent," CHS Hedging said in a note.

  • CBOT January soybeans (SF27) ended up 5-1/2 cents at $11.93-3/4 per bushel after falling earlier to the lowest level since August 12 at $11.84.

  • For the week, the contract tumbled 3.3%.

  • CBOT December soyoil (BOZ26) ended 0.02 cent higher at 62.26 cents per pound after sinking earlier to the lowest price since March 23.

  • CBOT December soymeal (SMZ26) closed up $2 at $319.20 per ton.

data.title: Mercedes-Benz bets on India luxury demand, EV push; plans 12 new models in 2026: Inside the company's growth strategy
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 6 -- Mercedes-Benz is betting on India's expanding luxury car market and growing demand for premium electric vehicles as it looks to strengthen its presence in the country.

The German automaker sees significant room to scale up its business over the next five to seven years and expects India to deliver a record year, according to company executives.

The company's latest electric SUV, the GLC EV, has received more than 1,000 bookings, taking its order book through March 2027, the Financial Express reported.

The strong initial response has prompted Mercedes-Benz India to approach its global leadership for additional assembly kits to ramp up local production and reduce waiting periods, the report said.

The India push comes amid a challenging global environment for the luxury carmaker, which is planning to introduce 12 new models in the country in 2026.

The GLC EV, priced at an introductory Rs.78.5 lakh (ex-showroom), is locally assembled at Mercedes-Benz India's Pune facility. Deliveries to the first set of customers are expected to begin shortly, according to the Financial Express report.

"We have got 1,000-plus bookings of this SUV now," Santosh Iyer, managing director and chief executive officer of Mercedes-Benz India, said at the vehicle's launch in Pune, as per the Financial Express report.

Iyer said the company was in discussions with its global leadership to secure additional assembly kits and increase production in India.

"I think this is going to be a record year, and there is no doubt that India has more potential for us," Mercedes-Benz Group Chairman Ola Kallenius told CNBC-TV18.

The company sold more than 5,400 vehicles in India in the third quarter of 2026, marking its best-ever quarterly performance in the country, Kallenius said.

He added that stronger-than-expected pre-orders for the electric GLC had reinforced the company's confidence in the market.

Mercedes-Benz is pursuing what Kallenius described as the biggest product launch offensive in its history, with 12 new models planned for India this year.

The strategy is aimed at tapping demand across the luxury vehicle segment, including electric cars. The company expects India's growing premium vehicle market to offer opportunities for expansion over the coming years.

The automaker is also looking to increase the number of models assembled at its Pune manufacturing facility and scale up production in line with demand.

Mercedes-Benz's expansion plans in India come as the company faces pressure in other key markets, particularly China, where demand for luxury goods and vehicles has weakened.

The company's revenue reportedly fell 9% last year, while adjusted operating profit declined 15% in the third quarter. It has also lowered its full-year outlook.

Kallenius said Mercedes-Benz had recorded growth outside China in each of the first three quarters of 2026, supported by new products. In China, the company is adapting its offerings to local consumer preferences and expanding research and development activity rather than scaling back its presence.

Mercedes-Benz's India strategy extends beyond vehicle sales to manufacturing, research and development, and partnerships with local suppliers and technology companies.

The company has invested more than Rs.3,000 crore in India, Kallenius said in his interview with CNBC-TV18.

It plans to add more models to its Pune facility and expand local production as demand grows.

While its current vehicle assembly operations are focused on the Indian market, Mercedes-Benz is also working with Indian suppliers and technology partners on its global operations.

data.title: Cleveland-Cliffs Reaches New Four-Year Labor Agreements with United Steelworkers
data.description:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. () today announced that it has reached new four-year labor agreements with the United Steelworkers (USW) across its operating footprint. The agreements cover approximately 12,000 USW-represented employees across the Company’s steel plants and mining operations in Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Minnesota, and Michigan. The agreements resolve all USW labor contracts currently up for renewal.

Lourenco Goncalves, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Cleveland-Cliffs, said: “Our USW-represented employees do work that is essential to Cleveland-Cliffs and to our country. These agreements recognize their contributions and give us the stability we need to invest, compete and continue strengthening American steelmaking. We greatly value our partnership with the USW and its leadership, whose constructive approach allowed us to reach agreements that benefit our employees and Cliffs.”

The new four-year agreements are subject to ratification by USW local union memberships.

About Cleveland-Cliffs Inc.

Cleveland-Cliffs is a leading North America-based steel producer with focus on value-added sheet products, particularly for the automotive industry. The Company is vertically integrated from the mining of iron ore, production of pellets and direct reduced iron, and processing of ferrous scrap through primary steelmaking and downstream finishing, stamping, tooling, and tubing. Headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio, Cleveland-Cliffs employs approximately 25,000 people across its operations in the United States and Canada.

data.title: Congo says US minerals deal should be judged by projects, not signed deals
data.description:
Key points:
  • Minister says Congo wants local mineral processing, wider electricity access, and peace
  • Paris meeting reviewed Lobito Corridor, Grand Inga project, joint statement
  • Statement cites growing American private-sector interest and expanding investment pipeline

Democratic Republic of Congo called on the United States on Friday to deliver concrete investments under their strategic minerals partnership, saying the success of the agreement should be measured by completed projects rather than signed deals.

"Our requirement is to move from signed agreements to real investments," Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba said on X.

"The success of the agreement must be measured by completed projects," Mukoko Samba said, adding that Congo wanted the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the country's east.

He made the comment after the second meeting of the joint steering committee overseeing the partnership, held in Paris.

In a joint statement after Mukoko Samba's post, Congo and the US said they were making progress under the partnership, citing growing American private-sector interest and an expanding investment pipeline.

"Both governments look forward to turning the strategic partnership agreement's commitments into lasting investment that creates jobs, strengthens supply chains, and brings shared prosperity to the American and Congolese peoples," the statement said.

Washington and Kinshasa signed the strategic minerals partnership in 2025, aiming to expand US access to Congo's vast copper, cobalt and other critical mineral resources in exchange for investment in mining, infrastructure and initiatives to support stability in the conflict-hit eastern Congo.

Despite ongoing insecurity in eastern Congo, the partnership has delivered some early gains, including the establishment of US-backed miner Virtus Minerals, increased Congolese copper exports to the US and investment in the Lobito Corridor, which will help transport minerals from central Africa to global markets through Angola's Atlantic coast.

In the statement, both governments said the US International Development Finance Corporation had briefed participants on its growing investment pipeline in Congo and welcomed increasing US private-sector interest in the country's strategic asset reserve programme.

The implementing committee cited progress on designated strategic projects, including the signing of a concession agreement for the Lobito Corridor, discussions on the Grand Inga hydropower project and opportunities for US companies in critical minerals processing, exports and energy.

The statement did not announce new investment commitments or identify specific projects expected to receive financing.

Congo, the world's largest cobalt producer and second-largest copper producer, is key to Washington’s push to reduce dependence on Chinese-dominated mineral supply chains.

data.description:
Google has acquired Crusoe's data center site in southeast Wyoming, the AI infrastructure developer said on Friday, a day after the Alphabet unit announced a $17-billion investment in the project.

Here are some details:

  • Google announced the investment on Thursday to build its first data center in Wyoming, expanding its AI infrastructure despite growing political opposition to such projects in parts of the US

  • Crusoe said it has completed its involvement in the project's pre-development phase, which included site selection, government approvals and power strategy

  • The deal's financial terms were not disclosed

  • The campus was initially developed by Crusoe and Tallgrass Energy

  • Google on Thursday said it would build the facility in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, as well as Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital

  • Crusoe Chief Executive Chase Lochmiller said the company has more than 6 gigawatts of contracted capacity and over 40 gigawatts in its development pipeline

  • Crusoe added that it is developing another Google data center campus in Armstrong, which it announced earlier this year

data.title: Torrent Gold to Acquire Sunset Tungsten Project
data.description:
Vancouver, British Columbia--(Newsfile Corp. - November 6, 2026) - Torrent Gold Inc. (FSE: RV00) ("Torrent" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that it has entered into a membership interest purchase agreement (the "Purchase Agreement"), dated November 6th, 2026, with Lamina Minerals LLC and Belle Morgan Ltd. (together, the "Vendors"). Pursuant to the Purchase Agreement, the Company proposes to acquire a series of nineteen unpatented lode mining claims located in Hidalgo County, New Mexico and commonly known as the "Sunrise Tungsten Project" (together, the "Project").

In consideration for the Project, the Company has agreed to: (i) complete a cash payment of Cdn$100,000, (ii) issue 3,500,000 common shares (the "Consideration Shares") and, (iii) grant a one-and-one-half percent (1.5%) net smelter returns royalty (the "Royalty") on commercial production from the Project, to the Vendors. The Company will be entitled to purchase three-quarters-of-one percent (0.75%) of the Royalty, at any time within ten years of closing, for a one-time cash payment of US$1,000,000.

The Company is at arms-length from each of the Vendors. No finders' fees or commissions are payable by the Company in connection with completion of the transaction contemplated by the Purchase Agreement. The Consideration Shares will be subject to a statutory hold period of four months and one day from the date of issuance, in accordance with applicable Canadian securities laws and such other further restrictions as may apply under foreign securities laws.

The transaction contemplated by the Purchase Agreement will constitute a "major acquisition" for the Company, in accordance with the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange, on the basis that it is expected to comprise the majority of the operating assets of the Company in the twelve month period following closing. As a result, completion of the transaction will be subject to the approval of the Canadian Securities Exchange. The transaction is not expected to result in a "Change of Control" for the Company, within the meaning prescribed by the policies of the Canadian Securities Exchange, nor is it expected to result in any changes to the board of directors or management of the Company,

About Torrent Gold Inc.

Torrent Gold is a mineral and natural resources exploration company that leverages its years of combined experience in capital markets and mining for acquisition and exploration during the resource commodity cycles.

data.title: Readers Remember Their Favorite Small Businesses — WSJ
data.description:
By Demetria Gallegos

My childhood neighborhood had two corner grocery stores within a few blocks of our home. I could go to either one with the quarters I had found under the sofa (and on my dad's dresser) and get some candy. A windfall might net me a mini fruit pie. And the independence of it was half the magic.

Today, children are more likely to have to go to a chain grocery store for candy, and odds are they'd have to be driven there, and escorted through the purchase by a reproving adult.

The kinds of small businesses and experiences that we cherished in the past are harder to find these days, and Wall Street Journal readers think something consequential has been lost.

We asked them, "Tell us about small businesses you remember fondly. What do you miss most about them?" Here are some of their answers. And a few of the beloved places that are still holding on.

Yearning for a plain old sandwich

I remember seeing independent sandwich shops everywhere. These weren't gourmet sandwiches or full-scale delis by any stretch of the imagination, but were places that you could get a good sandwich basket with chips, maybe some soup, and enjoy an affordable lunch at a nonchain restaurant.

Sure, New York City and Chicago still have many such places that also double as classic delis. But in my hometown of Kansas City, all the sandwich shops are now chain locations or have upscaled to something beyond a routine sandwich by offering organic/farm-fresh (read: expensive) odd takes on traditional sandwiches. What happened to these places? — Dillon Evans, Kansas City, Mo.

Know-it-alls (in a good way)

My father worked as a salesman for over 35 years at the original Black & Company Hardware Store on N. Water Street in Decatur, Ill., beginning in 1944. While the business is still in operation as an industrial and safety equipment supplier and has expanded to other cities, then it was a classic local hardware store, composed of two large rooms.

One room had squeaky, thin-slat wooden floors that housed a small department store assortment of dishes, kitchen appliances, tools, fans — just about anything a house would need. Shelves were packed with goods but well organized. A high shelf containing larger items ringed the room and was accessible only by a ladder. The other larger room contained building supplies including lumber, and large bins filled with commonly used nails, etc., as well as bins containing various types of seeds.

What stood out was the knowledge base of the clerks. My father and the others could give a dissertation on different types of screws: steel, stainless steel, iron, aluminum, thread angles and thickness, and on and on. It was a small work family of men and women who stayed on the job for years, worked as a team and tried to provide excellent service. If someone walked in the door one minute before closing, they were still provided with the same service even if it took half an hour.

My father was very outgoing and wherever we went in town, he would meet and chat with Black's regular customers. We had to allow at least an extra 15 minutes to get from our parking spot to wherever we wanted to go if we needed to be on time. Even after my father retired, he was warmly greeted by former customers for the remainder of his life. — Mark Ridlen, Wakefield, R.I.

My world in two blocks

Growing up in the Logan neighborhood of Philadelphia there was a group of food stores two blocks from my home. The seafood store had a table with raised sides and carp swimming in it. Next to it was a dairy store where cream cheese was cut from large slabs. The bread store was next to the bakery, and the butcher shop's floor was thick with sawdust.

In the middle of the block was Ulitsky's Deli, which had pickle barrels and every deli food in the world. There were two hair salons, a dress shop and a pharmacy. I loved being there, walking from store to store. It's still vivid, and I'm 98. — Edward Jawer, Wyncote, Pa.

Their name on the door

The small businesses of my suburban childhood in Summit, N.J., are still vivid in my mind. Each was run by its namesake: Scotti's Record Shop, where Mr. Scotti sold me my first record, "Heartbreak Hotel." Louvis's Luncheonette, the place we would all congregate for vanilla Cokes after school, until Mr. Louvis kicked us out. Rogers Pharmacy — he knew us all by first names and the meds we needed.

What strikes me now is that the founders of these beloved small businesses not only ran their own shops. It was not only that they knew everyone in town, although that gave us a comfort level you simply cannot find at the supermarket checkout counter, even though the clerk "knows" you. These beloved shops were an extension of the owners themselves. If they closed, we were devastated, as if we'd lost a family member. — Ellen Geiger, Andover, Mass.

Graphic memory

There was a comic-book store named Copacetic Comics in Pittsburgh, in the Polish Hill neighborhood, that was up two (very narrow) flights of stairs. It specialized in graphic novels from independent publishers and the gentleman who ran it gave a strong impression of having read everything in the store. You would pick up a book, and he would explain how the author had taken five years to paint all of the images in it.

I always felt so lucky to have a store like that in my city because of the unique, deep knowledge of the owner and the thoughtful selection of what was on display in the tiny store. — Mary E. Carter, Pittsburgh

Cheap, good eats

I miss the buffets on Fremont Street in Vegas in the 1970s. I used to go there for trade shows. I'd take a run in the early morning, then hit the buffet, with time to spare to get to our booth. I used to love showing that $2.95 buffet receipt to my company on my expense report.

The buffets were wonderful — much better than any hotel restaurant I ever stayed in. That they were cheaper was a bonus. Close, cheap, good. What's not to like? You didn't have to be a guest. They were open to the public.

Honestly, it was all of an era with regular visitors getting rooms "comped," and waitresses bringing drinks on the house if you sat at a slot long enough. Two-dollar blackjack tables. Nickel slots. Free parking. A weekend in Las Vegas could cost little more than what you left behind in the casino, and your casino chip was currency all over town. — Mike Knudsen, Trabuco Canyon, Calif.

I still remember the smell

Perhaps the most iconic small business in my hometown of Arlington, Va., was Ayers Hardware, which announced in July that it would be shutting its doors after almost 80 years. When I went to the Arlington Reddit to commiserate with my fellow Arlingtonians, the commenters read my mind. I immediately spotted a reply saying the user could practically smell the place just by seeing a picture.

When I was a kid, my friends and I would go in with a few dollars of cash and be able to buy tons of candy, some of which was so "vintage" it was impossible to find elsewhere. The place had a relaxed vibe with friendly employees, and I'd say what I miss most is that it didn't feel "optimized."

I find newer stores are sterile, cheaply designed efficiency factories to get customers in and out at record pace, where patrons could go 10 trips without speaking to another person. Perhaps those kinds of stores are more profitable and thus will beat out small businesses in the long run, but it leaves you missing something. — Jack Fisher, Arlington, Va.

Anchor store

I miss the 5 & 10. It was just this eclectic little store that had a bit of everything. As a kid, it was a rite of passage to be old enough to walk to the 5 & 10 to get some type of random candy — Razzles for me, why I have no idea — and to browse the makeup I hoped to someday be old enough to wear.

Once that store departed from Bedford Avenue in my small hometown of Bellmore, N.Y., it seemed it wasn't long before all the mainstays that had been there from the beginning were gone soon after (including the grocery store that burned down, the bakery, and the men's clothing store where my grandfather bought his fedoras). — Melissa Mauro Hineman, Charleston, S.C.

No more house calls

I miss the nostalgia of the milk man delivering glass gallon jugs to our home in open wooden crates, and how we'd leave the old glass jugs out for him to recycle.

Also, the knife sharpener and floor polisher who made house calls. Most of all, I miss our family doctor who came to our home and who knew us all by name, along with our medical history, without having to look at his chart. — Leslie Price, Rockville Centre, N.Y.

Another milk memory

I remember drive-through dairies near our home in Fontana, Calif. They mostly sold milk products, but I seem to recall free Popsicles for the kids in the car. We could also ride our bikes to one near our house, and pick up the milk. Our single mom worked, so this was probably a help to her. — Patty Smith, San Luis Obispo, Calif.

Side hustle

I miss the corner candy store or luncheonettes of my early life in Brooklyn and Long Island. They had soda fountains, a grill, newspapers, magazines, stationery, toys, playing cards and some necessities. These stores also had at least two pay phones.

I spent a lot of birthday money and allowance buying small chess sets, Spaulding balls and malteds at these establishments.

Later on, I learned that some of the proprietors also had a sideline...taking bets. — Charles-Eric Gordon, Plainview, N.Y.
